title: A Day in the Life of a Medieval Peasant
central_question: You owe the lord your harvest days and your flour. How much of your own life is actually yours?
setting: The same Midlands manor, c. 1260, at harvest (late August). Flash-forward to St Albans, 1331 and 1381.

lines.text: In 1331, an abbot set his town's hand mills into his floor.
How does a hand mill end up underfoot? Start your day at dawn.
Dawn. Somebody is hammering on your door.
Up! It's a boon day. The whole household, in the lord's field!
Today you work for the lord. For free.

badges.text: You, Walter the reeve and this day are fictional

cards.title: A Day in the Life of a Medieval Peasant

lines.text: At harvest, every household owed the lord extra days of reaping.
Sickle in one hand, stalks in the other. Cut. Bind. Stack. All day.
Walter the reeve, a neighbour the village chose, notches it on his tally.

badges.text: Reeves kept accounts with tally sticks

lines.text: The good news? On boon days, the lord had to feed you.
Bread. Cheese. Bacon, if you were lucky. And ale.
Manor records literally sorted the days into 'ale' boons...
...and 'dry' boons.

badges.text: Harvest meals at the lord's cost

lines.text: Sunset. You've gleaned some grain of your own.
So you grind it at home on your hand mill, the quern. What could go wrong?
Is that a hand mill? In this house?
On many manors, you had to grind at the lord's mill, and hand him a cut of your grain.
Home grinding dodged his fee. So lords banned hand mills.

badges.text: Suit of mill: his cut was often ~1/16

lines.text: In 1331, the abbot of St Albans seized the town's hand mills...
...and set the millstones into the floor of his parlour. As a 'memorial'.

cards.title: St Albans Abbey, 1331
cards.sub: Seventy years after your day in the field

lines.text: So the abbey walked on the town's querns. Every day.

badges.text: The abbot's look and the room are our reconstruction

lines.text: Fifty years later came the revolt of 1381...
...the townsfolk prised up those stones and smashed them.
Then they handed out the pieces like blessed bread at church.
Back home, you hide the quern under the straw.
Your field. Your flour. Your rules. For tonight.
Next time: you become a Roman gladiator.

badges.text: Hiding the quern: our story, not a record

claims.text: Boon-works (precariae, 'bedrips'): extra harvest days owed by the whole household (custumals often exempted the wife), on top of week-work; the lord fed the workers.
The reeve was usually a villein, often elected by the township for a year (Seneschaucy, c.1270s), sometimes appointed; works were counted on tally sticks alongside written accounts.
Boon-work meals at the lord's cost: bread, cheese, sometimes bacon, and ale (Birrell 2015; Dyer).

Records distinguish boon-days with ale from 'dry' ones: Anglo-Norman 'ale' and 'sec' bederep ('ale bedereps', 1298); Latin precariae siccae; the Ruislip custumal (by 1248) has 'water' vs 'ale' days. 'Wet boon' itself is NOT attested and is not used.
Querns (hand mills) were used to grind grain at home and persisted alongside lords' mills.
Suit of mill: tenants owed grinding at the lord's mill and paid multure, often reckoned around 1/16 (1/13 for unfree tenants in some northern manors).
Lords tried to suppress hand mills; St Albans Abbey banned them on its manors or required licences.

c.1331 Abbot Richard of Wallingford forced St Albans townspeople to surrender their hand mills and set the stones into the floor of the parlour (its doorway) 'as a record and memorial' (Thomas Walsingham).
The top-down layout of the floor, the number of stones shown and people walking over them are our reconstruction.

On 15 June 1381 rebels prised up the millstones, broke them and distributed the pieces 'as the bread that has been blessed is distributed... in the parochial churches' (Walsingham). Accounts of the aftermath vary.
You, Walter the reeve, Agnes, Tom, the dialogue and this day are fictional; the hidden quern is our story.

titles: Why Grinding Your Own Flour Was Banned
The Abbot Who Paved His Floor With Hand Mills
Medieval Workdays Came in Two Types: Ale or Dry
publishing.description: Your day starts with a reeve hammering on the door and ends with a hand mill you're not allowed to own. In between: free work for the lord, a lunch the lord had to pay for (with or without ale, and the records say which), and the abbot of St Albans, who set his town's confiscated hand mills into his floor.

publishing.whats_real: What's real: boon-work, the lord's mill and its fee, the ban on hand mills, and the St Albans floor of 1331 and its smashing in 1381 are documented history (sources below); the floor's exact look is a reconstruction. You, Walter the reeve, Agnes, Tom and the dialogue are fiction, and labelled on screen.
